concepts.statement: Diversification removes unsystematic risk, the part specific to individual securities. What remains in a well-diversified portfolio is systematic risk, which beta measures and which no amount of diversification can remove.
An option premium is intrinsic value plus time value. A put's intrinsic value is the excess of strike over spot (zero if spot is higher); whatever of the premium is not intrinsic value is time value.

concepts.subsection: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
concepts.statement: Under interest rate parity, the currency with the higher interest rate trades at a forward discount and the lower-rate currency at a forward premium, by the interest differential — otherwise borrowing in one currency and depositing in the other would be a free profit.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

concepts.statement: Duration measures a bond's price sensitivity to interest rate changes. It rises with maturity and falls with coupon; a zero-coupon bond's duration equals its maturity, the maximum for any bond of that term.

concepts.subsection: Section 54 — Capital gains on residential property
concepts.statement: Section 54 exempts long-term capital gains on the transfer of a residential house only when the gain is reinvested in a residential house in India — purchased within one year before or two years after the transfer, or constructed within three years. Reinvestment in commercial property earns no exemption.

Tax audit applies to a business at turnover above ₹1 crore, but the limit rises to ₹10 crore where cash receipts and cash payments each stay within 5 per cent of the respective totals. For a profession the limit is gross receipts above ₹50 lakh.

A domestic company that opts for section 115BAA pays tax at the concessional rate, must give up the specified deductions and incentives, and is outside MAT entirely — book profit tax does not apply to it at all.

A company files its return by 31 October of the assessment year. Where it must furnish a transfer pricing report under section 92E, the due date extends to 30 November. The 31 July date belongs to persons with no audit requirement.

Long-term capital gains on listed equity shares where STT is paid are taxed under section 112A above an annual exemption threshold, without indexation. The rate and threshold are Finance Act figures and move; the structure — exemption slab, no indexation, STT condition — is the stable part.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 115 — Revenue from Contracts with Customers
concepts.statement: Revenue is recognised when (or as) a performance obligation is satisfied by transferring control of the promised good or service to the customer. Transfer of control, not transfer of risks and rewards, is the recognition trigger.
Inventories of items that are not ordinarily interchangeable are costed by specific identification. For the rest, FIFO or weighted average is used. LIFO is not permitted.
An asset is impaired when its carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount, and recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use.

An investor controls an investee only when it has all three elements together — power over the investee, exposure or rights to variable returns, and the ability to use its power to affect those returns. Control does not require a majority shareholding.

Loss allowances are measured on an expected credit loss basis, recognised from initial recognition without waiting for a default. For trade receivables the simplified approach applies, and the allowance is always lifetime expected credit losses.

Under the Indian carve-out, a gain on a bargain purchase is recognised in other comprehensive income and accumulated in capital reserve, not in profit or loss — unlike IFRS 3, which takes it to profit or loss.

concepts.subsection: Going concern across FR and audit
concepts.statement: Material uncertainties about going concern are disclosed in the financial statements themselves — Ind AS 1 requires it of management when it is aware of them. A mention in the board's report or a covering letter is not a substitute, and the auditor's going concern section points to the note, so the note must exist.

concepts.subsection: Related party transactions under company law
concepts.statement: A contract with a related party of the kinds listed in section 188 — sale or purchase of goods, property, services, agency — needs board approval by resolution when it is not in the ordinary course of business or not at arm's length, and shareholder approval past the prescribed thresholds. An interested director does not participate.

A chartered accountant in practice cannot charge professional fees as a percentage of profits or contingent on results, outside the specific exceptions the Council has carved out — an auditor paid a share of what he certifies has bought a stake in the number.

Input tax credit needs every section 16(2) condition together — a tax invoice, receipt of the goods or services, the detail appearing in GSTR-2B, the tax actually paid to the Government by the supplier, and the return filed. Holding a valid invoice while the supplier has not paid the tax defeats the credit.

Input tax credit on motor vehicles for transporting persons, with seating capacity up to thirteen, is blocked — unless the vehicle is used for further supply of vehicles, transport of passengers, or driver training. Ordinary business use of a car is not an exception.

For notified supplies — legal services from an advocate to a business entity among them — the recipient, not the supplier, is liable to pay the tax, and pays it in cash rather than through input tax credit.

Registration becomes compulsory when aggregate turnover crosses ₹20 lakh for a supplier of services. The ₹40 lakh limit is for suppliers exclusively of goods in eligible States, and special category States carry lower limits.

A composition taxpayer cannot make inter-State outward supplies of goods. The scheme trades a small turnover-based levy for staying local; crossing the State line with outward supplies forfeits eligibility.

Additions to the transaction value of imported goods include selling commissions, and cost of transport and insurance to the place of importation — but buying commission, paid to the importer's own agent for representing him abroad, is not added.

concepts.subsection: SA 200 — Overall Objectives of the Independent Auditor
concepts.statement: An audit conducted under the Standards on Auditing obtains reasonable assurance, which is a high level of assurance but not absolute assurance.

concepts.subsection: SA 210 — Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements
concepts.statement: The preconditions for an audit are an acceptable financial reporting framework and management's agreement to the premise on which an audit is conducted — its responsibility for the financial statements, for internal control, and for giving the auditor access and information. Where the preconditions are not present, the auditor does not accept the engagement.

concepts.subsection: SA 210 — Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements
concepts.statement: Where management imposes a limitation on scope before the engagement is accepted, and the auditor expects that limitation will result in a disclaimer of opinion, the auditor does not accept the engagement unless law or regulation requires it.

concepts.subsection: SA 220 (Revised) — Quality Management for an Audit
concepts.statement: The engagement partner takes overall responsibility for managing and achieving quality on the engagement. Work may be delegated across the engagement team, but the responsibility for quality is not delegated with it.
The final audit file is assembled ordinarily within not more than 60 days after the date of the auditor's report.

concepts.subsection: SA 240 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud
concepts.statement: Management override of controls is a significant risk presumed to be present in every audit, and it is not rebuttable.

concepts.subsection: SA 240 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud
concepts.statement: There is a presumed risk of fraud in revenue recognition, and unlike management override that presumption may be rebutted with documented reasons.

concepts.subsection: SA 250 — Consideration of Laws and Regulations
concepts.statement: SA 250 splits laws into two categories, and the auditor's responsibility differs between them. For laws with a direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures, the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence about compliance. For other laws that are fundamental to the operating aspects of the business, the auditor only performs specified procedures to help identify non-compliance.

concepts.subsection: SA 260 (Revised) — Communication with Those Charged with Governance
concepts.statement: The auditor communicates the planned scope and timing of the audit to those charged with governance, not only the findings.

concepts.subsection: SA 265 — Communicating Deficiencies in Internal Control
concepts.statement: Significant deficiencies in internal control are communicated in writing to those charged with governance on a timely basis.

concepts.subsection: SA 299 (Revised) — Joint Audit of Financial Statements
concepts.statement: Each joint auditor is responsible for the work divided to that auditor, and all joint auditors are jointly and severally responsible for the work not divided.

concepts.subsection: SA 315 (Revised) — Identifying and Assessing the Risks of Material Misstatement
concepts.statement: A significant risk is one requiring special audit consideration, and for such risks the auditor must obtain an understanding of the entity's related controls.

concepts.subsection: SA 320 — Materiality in Planning and Performing an Audit
concepts.statement: Performance materiality is set below materiality for the financial statements as a whole, to reduce to an appropriately low level the probability that uncorrected and undetected misstatements aggregate above materiality.

concepts.subsection: SA 330 — The Auditor's Responses to Assessed Risks
concepts.statement: When the auditor has determined that an assessed risk of material misstatement at the assertion level is a significant risk, substantive procedures specifically responsive to that risk must be performed.

concepts.subsection: SA 402 — Audit Considerations Relating to an Entity Using a Service Organisation
concepts.statement: A Type 1 report describes the service organisation's system and the design of its controls at a point in time. A Type 2 report also reports on their operating effectiveness over a period. Only a Type 2 report can give evidence about operating effectiveness.

concepts.subsection: SA 450 — Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit
concepts.statement: Uncorrected misstatements are communicated to those charged with governance and the auditor evaluates whether they are material individually or in aggregate.
Sufficiency is the measure of the quantity of audit evidence; appropriateness is the measure of its quality, being its relevance and its reliability.

concepts.subsection: SA 501 — Audit Evidence: Specific Considerations for Selected Items
concepts.statement: When inventory is material to the financial statements, the auditor must attend the physical inventory counting unless it is impracticable.

Negative confirmations may be used as the sole substantive procedure only when the assessed risk is low, the population is large and homogeneous, a very low exception rate is expected, and the auditor is not aware of circumstances that would cause recipients to disregard them.

concepts.subsection: SA 510 — Initial Audit Engagements: Opening Balances
concepts.statement: In an initial audit engagement the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence about whether opening balances contain misstatements that materially affect the current period's financial statements, and whether accounting policies reflected in the opening balances have been consistently applied.

Analytical procedures are mandatory at two points in an audit — as risk assessment procedures during planning, and near the end of the audit to form an overall conclusion. Using them as substantive procedures is optional, a choice the auditor makes about how to respond to an assessed risk.

Misstatements found in a sample are projected to the population the sample was drawn from. The sample is a means of reaching a conclusion about the whole population, so the error found in it is evidence about the whole population, not only about the items examined.

A significant related party transaction outside the entity's normal course of business gives rise to a significant risk. The auditor inspects the underlying contracts and evaluates whether the business rationale suggests the transaction was entered into to engage in fraudulent financial reporting or to conceal misappropriation of assets.
Where the report is amended for a subsequent event, dual dating confines the auditor's responsibility for events after the original date to that amendment alone.

Where a material uncertainty about going concern exists and is adequately disclosed, the opinion is unmodified and a separate section headed "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern" is included.

Written representations are audit evidence, but they are not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own about any of the matters they deal with. Obtaining them does not affect the nature or extent of the other evidence the auditor obtains.

concepts.subsection: SA 600 — Using the Work of Another Auditor
concepts.statement: Where a principal auditor uses the work of another auditor for a component, the principal auditor states the division of responsibility in the audit report, indicating the extent of the financial information audited by the other auditor. The principal auditor is not responsible for the work entrusted to the other auditor, except where circumstances should have aroused suspicion about its reliability.

concepts.subsection: SA 610 (Revised) — Using the Work of Internal Auditors
concepts.statement: SA 610 (Revised) permits internal auditors to provide direct assistance under the external auditor's direction, supervision and review — but never for procedures that involve significant judgments, relate to higher assessed risks where more than limited judgment is required, or cover work the internal audit function has itself reported on. Written agreements from the entity and the internal auditors come first.

concepts.subsection: SA 620 — Using the Work of an Auditor's Expert
concepts.statement: The auditor has sole responsibility for the audit opinion, and that responsibility is not reduced by using the work of an auditor's expert. The auditor's report does not refer to the expert unless the reference is required by law or regulation, and where it is, the report must state that the reference does not reduce the auditor's responsibility.

concepts.subsection: SA 700 (Revised) — Forming an Opinion and Reporting
concepts.statement: The auditor's report presents the Opinion as its first section, and the Basis for Opinion comes directly after it. The conclusion is stated before the reasons for it, so a reader who stops after the first paragraph has still read the opinion.
Key audit matters are required for audits of complete sets of general purpose financial statements of listed entities, and where otherwise required by law or voluntarily undertaken.
A material misstatement that is not pervasive gives a qualified opinion; a material misstatement that is pervasive gives an adverse opinion.

concepts.subsection: SA 706 (Revised) — Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter Paragraphs
concepts.statement: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph refers to a matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements; an Other Matter paragraph refers to a matter not so disclosed but relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the report.

concepts.subsection: SA 710 — Comparative Information: Corresponding Figures and Comparative Financial Statements
concepts.statement: Where comparatives are presented as corresponding figures, the auditor's opinion refers to the current period only and does not refer to the corresponding figures. Where they are presented as comparative financial statements, the opinion refers to each period for which financial statements are presented.

concepts.subsection: SA 720 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Other Information
concepts.statement: The auditor reads the other information in the annual report and considers whether it is materially inconsistent with the financial statements or with the auditor's knowledge obtained in the audit. The auditor does not audit the other information and expresses no opinion or conclusion on it.

items.stem: Which risk is the portfolio still carrying?

options.text: Liquidity risk, since twelve industries cannot all be sold at once
options.misconception: substitutes a trading concern for the pricing question asked
options.why: Liquidity affects the cost of exiting, not why the valuation tracked the index. The co-movement with the market is systematic risk by definition.

options.text: Unsystematic risk, because thirty stocks are too few
options.misconception: believes firm-specific risk lingers until the portfolio holds the whole market
options.why: The gain from diversification flattens quickly — most firm-specific risk is gone well before thirty stocks. The 9 per cent fall tracking a 10 per cent market fall is market behaviour, not stock-picking noise.

options.text: None — a fall proves the portfolio was badly constructed
options.misconception: reads any loss as evidence of avoidable risk
options.why: A diversified portfolio is supposed to move with the market; that is what remains after the removable risk is removed. A loss in a falling market is the priced risk showing up.

options.text: Systematic risk, which diversification cannot remove
options.why: Thirty stocks across twelve industries has diversified away nearly all firm-specific risk. What moves the portfolio now is the market itself — interest rates, the cycle, policy — and that risk is common to every security, so holding more of them does not dilute it.

items.scenario: An investor holds a portfolio of 30 stocks spread across twelve industries and asks why its value still fell 9 per cent in a month when the market index fell 10 per cent.

items.stem: What are the put's intrinsic value and time value?

options.text: Intrinsic value nil, time value ₹11
options.misconception: applies the call test to a put and reads spot below strike as out of the money
options.why: For a call this spot would mean no intrinsic value, and that is the reflex being tested. A put gains when the share falls, so spot below strike is in the money.

options.text: Intrinsic value ₹11, time value nil
options.misconception: equates the whole premium with intrinsic value
options.why: The premium is the price of the option, not its exercise value. Intrinsic value comes from strike against spot alone, and here that is ₹8.

options.text: Intrinsic value ₹8, time value ₹3
options.why: The put lets its holder sell at ₹100 what the market prices at ₹92, so exercising now is worth ₹8 — the intrinsic value. The premium's remaining ₹3 is time value, paid for the chance the share falls further before expiry.

options.text: Intrinsic value ₹3, time value ₹8
options.misconception: swaps the two components
options.why: The split runs the other way. Exercise value first — strike ₹100 less spot ₹92 — and only the remainder of the premium is time value.

items.scenario: A put option on a share has a strike price of ₹100. The share trades at ₹92 and the put's premium is ₹11.

items.stem: Where must the one-year forward rate sit, relative to spot?

options.text: Above ₹84 — the dollar at a forward premium, the rupee at a discount
options.why: A depositor could otherwise convert to rupees, earn 7 per cent against 3, and convert back with nothing lost. The forward rate removes that free profit by making future dollars dearer — roughly by the 4 per cent differential, near ₹87.2.

options.text: Below ₹84 — the rupee at a forward premium because its interest rate is higher
options.misconception: gives the forward premium to the high-rate currency
options.why: This is parity read backwards. The higher rate is compensation for the currency expected to weaken; if the rupee also strengthened forward, holding rupees would win twice and arbitrage would close the gap at once.

options.text: It depends only on expected inflation in the two countries
options.misconception: answers with purchasing power parity when the question fixes interest rates
options.why: Inflation drives the long-run story through PPP, but the covered forward rate is pinned by interest rate parity — the rates given are the whole calculation.

options.text: Exactly ₹84, because forward rates track spot when markets are efficient
options.misconception: treats efficiency as making the interest differential irrelevant
options.why: Efficiency is what forces the gap open, not shut. A forward equal to spot with a 4 per cent rate differential is a money machine, and efficient markets price it away.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: One-year interest rates are 7 per cent in India and 3 per cent in the United States. The spot rate is ₹84 per dollar. Markets are free of arbitrage.

items.stem: A fund expects interest rates to fall and wants the largest price gain. Which bond should it hold?

options.text: A floating-rate bond resetting every six months
options.misconception: reaches for the bond that adjusts to rates rather than the one that gains from them
options.why: A floater's coupon resets to the market, so its price barely moves — near-zero duration. It is the instrument for avoiding the bet, not winning it.

options.text: A ten-year bond with a 12 per cent coupon
options.misconception: picks the highest coupon as the biggest gainer
options.why: Large coupons return money early, which shortens duration and dampens the price move. Same maturity, less sensitivity than the zero.

options.text: A ten-year zero-coupon bond
options.why: Price sensitivity follows duration, and a zero-coupon bond's duration equals its full maturity because every rupee arrives at the end. Ten years of duration is the most leverage to a rate fall among these choices.

options.text: A two-year zero-coupon bond
options.misconception: remembers zeros are sensitive but forgets maturity drives it
options.why: Being a zero helps only as far as the maturity allows. Two years of duration moves far less than ten when rates shift.

items.stem: Is he entitled to the section 54 exemption?

options.text: No, but he can claim it under section 54F instead
options.misconception: swaps in the section that runs in the opposite direction
options.why: Section 54F exempts gains on assets other than a residential house when the proceeds buy a residential house. Here the sale was residential and the purchase was not — the wrong way round for both sections.

options.text: Yes, because the amount invested exceeds the capital gain
options.misconception: reads the quantum condition and skips the nature-of-asset condition
options.why: The amount decides how much of the gain is exempt once the conditions are met. It cannot substitute for the condition that the new asset be a residential house.

options.text: Yes, if the shop is let out for residential use by the tenant
options.misconception: lets the tenant's use recharacterise the property
options.why: The character of the asset purchased is what it is — commercial premises. What a tenant does inside it does not turn a shop into a residential house for section 54.

options.text: No — the reinvestment must be in a residential house in India
options.why: Section 54 is an exemption for keeping capital in residential housing. Both ends of the transaction must be residential: the asset sold and the asset bought. A shop fails the second condition however large the investment.

items.scenario: An individual sells a residential house in June 2025, earning a long-term capital gain of ₹65 lakh. Within a year he invests ₹70 lakh in a commercial shop, arguing the whole gain is exempt because the reinvestment exceeds the gain.

items.stem: Is a tax audit under section 44AB required?

options.text: Yes, because turnover exceeds ₹1 crore
options.misconception: applies the base limit without testing for the digital-transactions proviso
options.why: ₹1 crore is the starting rule, and the proviso is the examinable part: heavy banking- channel usage lifts the limit tenfold precisely to spare businesses like this one.

options.text: Yes, because the limit for firms is ₹50 lakh
options.misconception: applies the professional gross-receipts limit to a business
options.why: ₹50 lakh is the threshold for a profession's gross receipts. A trading firm is a business and takes the business limits.

options.text: No, because audit under section 44AB applies only to companies
options.misconception: confuses tax audit with statutory audit under the Companies Act
options.why: Section 44AB turns on turnover, not on the form of the entity. Individuals, firms and companies are all within it; companies separately face statutory audit regardless.

options.text: No — the enhanced ₹10 crore limit applies because cash stays within 5 per cent
options.why: Where both cash receipts and cash payments are within 5 per cent of their totals, the audit threshold is ₹10 crore, not ₹1 crore. At ₹8 crore of largely digital turnover, no audit is required.

items.scenario: A trading firm has turnover of ₹8 crore for the year. Its cash receipts are 3 per cent of total receipts and cash payments are 2 per cent of total payments; everything else moves through banking channels.

items.stem: What is the MAT position of this company?

options.text: MAT applies at the standard rate on book profit, payable if higher
options.misconception: runs the MAT comparison out of habit for every company
options.why: The compare-and-pay-higher routine belongs to companies under the normal regime. For a 115BAA company there is nothing to compare — the computation itself is switched off.

options.text: MAT does not apply to it at all
options.why: Opting into 115BAA takes the company outside MAT entirely — section 115JB(5A) says the book profit provisions do not apply. The bargain is a lower flat rate in exchange for the incentives, and MAT has no role because there are no incentives left to claw back.

options.text: MAT applies, but unused MAT credit can be set off against it
options.misconception: keeps MAT credit alive inside a regime that has no MAT
options.why: Old MAT credit lapses on opting in — one of the real costs of the choice. There is no future MAT liability for the credit to meet.

options.text: MAT applies only if book profit exceeds taxable income by 20 per cent
options.misconception: invents a threshold test for when MAT switches on
options.why: No such trigger exists anywhere in the Act. Under the normal regime MAT is always computed; under 115BAA it never is.

items.scenario: A domestic company opted for section 115BAA two years ago. This year its book profit is high while its taxable income is modest, and the tax team begins computing MAT on book profit as a comparison.

items.stem: What is the due date?

options.text: 30 November 2026
options.misconception: extends the transfer pricing date to every company
options.why: 30 November applies only where a report under section 92E is required — international or specified domestic transactions. This company has none.

options.text: 30 September 2026
options.misconception: recalls the pre-amendment audit due date
options.why: 30 September was the audit-case date years ago and survives in old material. The current date is 31 October.

options.text: 31 July 2026
options.misconception: applies the no-audit individual due date to a company
options.why: 31 July belongs to taxpayers with no audit requirement. A company never files by this date.

options.text: 31 October 2026
options.why: A company is an audit case by definition for this purpose, and the due date for audit cases is 31 October of the assessment year.

items.scenario: A private limited company with no international or specified domestic transactions asks for the last date to file its income-tax return for assessment year 2026-27.

items.stem: Which statement describes the section 112A treatment?

options.text: Taxed with indexation benefit at the general long-term rate
options.misconception: applies the section 112 computation that 112A displaces
options.why: Indexation is the general regime's feature. Section 112A trades it away for the lower rate and the annual exempt slab.

options.text: Taxed above an annual exemption threshold at the special rate, without indexation
options.why: Section 112A carves listed STT-paid equity out of the general LTCG regime: a slab of gain each year is exempt, the excess is taxed at the concessional rate, and no indexation is available against it.

options.text: Taxed at normal slab rates like any other income
options.misconception: ignores the special regime entirely
options.why: Listed equity LTCG never meets slab rates while 112A stands; the section exists to give it its own rate and threshold.

options.text: Fully exempt, because STT was paid at both purchase and sale
options.misconception: remembers the pre-2018 section 10(38) exemption as still alive
options.why: The blanket exemption ended when 112A arrived. STT payment is now the condition for the concessional regime, not for exemption.

items.scenario: An investor sells listed equity shares after two years, through the exchange with STT paid, realising a long-term gain. She asks how the gain is taxed.

items.stem: How much revenue does the manufacturer recognise for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: Revenue for the 60 per cent the agent has sold to end customers
options.why: Control of consigned goods does not pass on despatch — the agent can return them and holds them for the manufacturer. Control passes when the agent sells to a customer, so only those units have satisfied a performance obligation under Ind AS 115.

options.text: Revenue spread evenly over the consignment period
options.misconception: converts a point-in-time obligation into an over-time one without meeting any criterion
options.why: Over-time recognition needs one of the Ind AS 115 criteria — the customer consuming the benefit as the entity performs, or the entity creating an asset the customer controls. A consignment of finished goods meets none of them.

options.text: Revenue for the full despatch, since the goods have left the premises
options.misconception: treats despatch as sale, the recognition trigger Ind AS 115 replaced
options.why: Despatch moves the goods, not control. The agent has no obligation to pay for unsold units and can return them, so the manufacturer still controls them.

options.text: No revenue until the agent remits the money
options.misconception: uses receipt of cash as the recognition trigger
options.why: Collection is a separate matter from recognition. Once control of a unit has passed to an end customer, the obligation is satisfied whether or not the agent has remitted.

items.scenario: A manufacturer despatches goods to a consignment agent on 28 March 2026. The agent holds the goods, can return any unsold units, and sells to end customers on the manufacturer's behalf. By 31 March the agent has sold 60 per cent of the units to customers.

items.stem: Which inventory cost formula does Ind AS 2 not permit?

options.text: Specific identification
options.misconception: forgets the formula required for non-interchangeable items
options.why: Specific identification is not merely permitted — it is required where items are not ordinarily interchangeable, such as goods segregated for a specific project.

options.text: LIFO
options.why: Ind AS 2 allows specific identification for non-interchangeable items, and FIFO or weighted average for the rest. LIFO is expressly not an option — in a rising price environment it books the newest, dearest cost first and leaves inventory at stale values.

options.text: Weighted average
options.misconception: assumes averaging is imprecise and therefore barred
options.why: Weighted average is the other permitted formula for interchangeable items.

options.text: FIFO
options.misconception: confuses the permitted default with the prohibited formula
options.why: FIFO is one of the two formulas permitted for interchangeable items.

items.stem: What impairment loss, if any, is recognised?

options.text: ₹9 lakh, but only if the fall is judged permanent
options.misconception: imports the old permanent-diminution test into Ind AS 36
options.why: Permanence is the older Indian GAAP idea. Ind AS 36 works from indicators and measurement, not from a judgement about whether the fall will last.

options.text: ₹9 lakh
options.why: Recoverable amount is the higher of the two measures — ₹91 lakh — because a rational owner would keep using an asset worth more in use than in sale. Carrying amount ₹100 lakh less ₹91 lakh gives a loss of ₹9 lakh.

options.text: ₹18 lakh
options.misconception: takes the lower of the two measures as recoverable amount
options.why: Using the lower figure (₹82 lakh) writes the asset below what the business can actually recover from it. The standard says higher, precisely to prevent this over-write-down.

options.text: Nil, because value in use exceeds fair value less costs of disposal
options.misconception: compares the two recoverable measures to each other instead of to carrying amount
options.why: The comparison that matters is recoverable amount against carrying amount. ₹91 lakh against ₹100 lakh still leaves a shortfall of ₹9 lakh.

items.scenario: A plant has a carrying amount of ₹100 lakh. Its fair value less costs of disposal is ₹82 lakh and its value in use is ₹91 lakh.

items.stem: Does the company control the investee under Ind AS 110?

options.text: No, but the investee is a joint venture
options.misconception: mislabels one-sided board control as joint control
options.why: Joint control requires unanimous consent of the sharing parties over relevant activities. A right to appoint four of seven directors is unilateral, not shared.

options.text: No, the 45 per cent holding gives significant influence and equity accounting
options.misconception: stops at the shareholding percentage and applies the associate test
options.why: Significant influence is the fallback when control is absent. Here the board rights give actual power, so the investee is a subsidiary and is consolidated.

options.text: No, because control requires holding more than half the voting power
options.misconception: equates control with majority shareholding
options.why: Majority voting power is one route to power, not the definition of it. Ind AS 110 was written precisely to catch control held through other means.

options.text: Yes — it has power through the board rights, variable returns, and the link between them
options.why: All three elements of control are present. Power does not have to come from a majority of shares; a contractual right to appoint the majority of the board directs the relevant activities just as effectively.

items.scenario: A company holds 45 per cent of the voting shares of an investee. A shareholders' agreement gives it the contractual right to appoint four of the seven directors, and its returns vary with the investee's performance.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 109 require instead?

options.text: An allowance once a receivable is more than 90 days overdue
options.misconception: imports the banking overdue norms into financial reporting
options.why: Ninety days is a prudential banking classification, not an Ind AS measurement rule. There is a rebuttable presumption of default at 90 days past due, but the allowance exists long before that.

options.text: A 12-month expected credit loss allowance unless credit risk has increased significantly
options.misconception: applies the general staging model where the simplified approach governs
options.why: The two-stage general model applies to loans and debt investments. Trade receivables take the simplified approach, which is lifetime losses without a staging test.

options.text: A lifetime expected credit loss allowance on trade receivables from initial recognition
options.why: Ind AS 109 replaced the incurred-loss model with expected credit losses, recognised before any default. For trade receivables the simplified approach removes the staging debate entirely — the allowance is always lifetime expected losses.

options.text: The company's policy is compliant, since losses should not be anticipated
options.misconception: defends the incurred-loss model the standard replaced
options.why: Waiting for the loss event is exactly what Ind AS 109 abolished. Expected losses are an estimate of the future, made from the first day the receivable exists.

items.scenario: A company recognises a loss allowance on trade receivables only when a customer has actually defaulted, on the ground that anything earlier would be providing for losses that have not happened.

items.stem: Where does the ₹8 crore gain go under Ind AS 103?

options.text: Other comprehensive income, accumulated in capital reserve
options.why: This is the Indian carve-out. IFRS 3 takes a bargain purchase gain to profit or loss; Ind AS 103 routes it through other comprehensive income into capital reserve, keeping a purchase discount out of earnings.

options.text: Reduced from the values of the assets acquired
options.misconception: treats the gain as a measurement error to be spread over assets
options.why: Reassessment happens first, and this scenario says it already has. Once the measurements stand, the difference is a recognised gain, not an allocation.

options.text: Deferred and amortised to profit or loss over five years
options.misconception: invents an amortisation treatment the standard does not contain
options.why: Nothing in Ind AS 103 spreads a bargain purchase gain over time. It is recognised at once, in other comprehensive income.

options.text: Profit or loss immediately
options.misconception: applies the IFRS 3 treatment where the Indian carve-out differs
options.why: Correct under IFRS 3, and the classic trap in an Ind AS paper. The carve-out exists precisely because recognising acquisition-day gains in earnings was thought unsuitable.

items.scenario: A company acquires a business for ₹70 crore when the fair value of identifiable net assets acquired is ₹78 crore. After reassessing the identification and measurement, the ₹8 crore difference remains.

items.stem: As auditor, what do you require before the report is signed?

options.text: A written representation from the CFO that the banks have been informed separately
options.misconception: routes a reporting defect into a representation
options.why: Whom the bankers heard from privately has no bearing on what the statements must say to every reader. And a representation is never sufficient evidence on its own, least of all about a disclosure that is visibly missing.

options.text: Disclosure of the material uncertainty in the notes to the financial statements themselves
options.why: Ind AS 1 puts the disclosure duty on the financial statements when management is aware of material uncertainties over going concern. The directors' report is not audited to the same standard and is not where SA 570's dedicated section can point. Without the note the statements are misstated, and the opinion — not just a paragraph — is what changes.

options.text: Nothing further, since the auditor's own going concern section will inform readers
options.misconception: uses the auditor's report to carry management's disclosure duty
options.why: The auditor's section draws attention to the note; it does not replace it. Where the note is absent, the statements are wrong and the response is a modified opinion, not a louder auditor's paragraph.

options.text: A more detailed description in the directors' report, cross-referenced from the audit report
options.misconception: accepts other-information disclosure as a substitute for the note
options.why: The directors' report is other information. A cross-reference from the audit report cannot cure an omission inside the statements — it would advertise the very gap it papers over.

items.scenario: A company has defaulted on its term loans and its net current liabilities are ₹80 crore. The CFO agrees a material uncertainty exists but proposes to describe it in the directors' report only, keeping the financial statements clean "so the bankers do not panic". The audit is in final review.

items.stem: What does section 188 require for this contract?

options.text: No approval, because buying fabric is the company's ordinary course of business
options.misconception: applies half the exemption and drops the arm's length half
options.why: The exemption needs both limbs: ordinary course and arm's length. An 8 per cent premium concedes the second limb, and one failed limb brings the section fully into play.

options.text: Only disclosure in the board's report, since the amount is below ₹50 crore
options.misconception: substitutes a disclosure threshold for the approval requirement
options.why: Thresholds decide when shareholders must approve on top of the board — they never reduce the requirement to disclosure alone. The board resolution is the floor, not the ceiling.

options.text: Approval of the Registrar of Companies before execution
options.misconception: sends a governance decision to the regulator
options.why: Section 188 keeps the decision inside the company — board, and shareholders where thresholds require. The Registrar receives filings; he does not approve contracts.

options.text: Board approval by resolution, with the interested director not participating
options.why: The counterparty is a related party and the pricing is not arm's length, so the ordinary- course-and-arm's-length exemption is unavailable. Section 188 then requires a board resolution — with shareholder approval as well if the prescribed thresholds are crossed — and the interested director stays out of the discussion and the vote.

items.scenario: A public company proposes to buy fabric worth ₹12 crore annually from a partnership in which a director's son is a partner, at prices about 8 per cent above the market, citing assured quality. The purchase committee asks what approvals the contract needs.

items.stem: Can the auditor accept this fee arrangement?

options.text: Yes, because fee structure is a private contract between auditor and client
options.misconception: places the engagement contract above the professional schedules
options.why: The Chartered Accountants Act sits over every engagement letter a member signs. A contract cannot authorise what the First Schedule defines as misconduct.

options.text: Yes, if the arrangement is disclosed to shareholders in the general meeting
options.misconception: treats disclosure as curing a prohibited arrangement
options.why: Disclosure cures conflicts that are permissible to hold. This one is prohibited outright; telling the shareholders about it only documents the misconduct.

options.text: No — fees contingent on results or based on a percentage of profits are prohibited
options.why: An auditor paid a share of the profit he certifies holds a stake in the number under audit. The First Schedule makes such fees professional misconduct, outside the narrow exceptions the Council has prescribed for specific engagements — statutory audit is not among them.

options.text: No, unless the percentage is capped at a maximum absolute amount
options.misconception: believes a ceiling converts a contingent fee into a fixed one
options.why: A capped percentage still rises and falls with the profits below the cap — the stake in the certified number remains. The defect is the linkage, not the size.

items.scenario: A client offers its statutory auditor a fee of 2 per cent of audited net profits, arguing it aligns the auditor's diligence with the company's success and is common for consultants.

items.stem: Can the company take the ₹7.2 lakh input tax credit?

options.text: No, and the goods must also be returned to the supplier
options.misconception: attaches a consequence to the goods when the defect is in the tax chain
options.why: The purchase itself is untouched — the goods are the company's. What fails is the credit; the company's remedy against the supplier is contractual, not a return of goods.

options.text: Yes — a valid invoice and receipt of goods complete the recipient's obligations
options.misconception: treats the recipient-side conditions as the whole test
options.why: That was the intuition under the old regime and it is the specific thing section 16(2)(c) rejects. The credit is of tax paid, and no tax was paid.

options.text: No — payment of the tax to the Government by the supplier is itself a condition
options.why: Section 16(2)(c) makes the supplier's actual payment a condition of the recipient's credit. Invoice, receipt and GSTR-2B appearance satisfy three conditions of five; all of them must hold together, and the missing one defeats the claim.

options.text: Yes, provisionally, reversible if the supplier stays in default for six months
options.misconception: recalls the provisional-credit mechanism that no longer exists
options.why: Provisional credit was removed from the law. Credit now follows GSTR-2B and the satisfied conditions, with no provisional window to occupy.

items.scenario: A company buys raw material worth ₹40 lakh plus ₹7.2 lakh GST, holds a valid tax invoice, has received the goods, and the invoice appears in its GSTR-2B. It then learns the supplier collected the tax but never deposited it with the Government.

items.stem: Is the credit available?

options.text: Yes, for half the credit, with the rest reversed
options.misconception: imports a proportionate formula where the block is absolute
options.why: Proportionate reversal belongs to mixed taxable-and-exempt use under section 17(2). A 17(5) block is complete, not partial.

options.text: No — credit on passenger vehicles up to thirteen seats is blocked, and business use is not an exception
options.why: Section 17(5)(a) blocks credit on such vehicles regardless of business purpose. The exceptions are dealing in vehicles, transporting passengers for consideration, and driver training — client visits are none of these.

options.text: Yes, because the car is used exclusively for business purposes
options.misconception: applies the general business-use test to a specifically blocked credit
options.why: Business use is the entry condition for all credit, and section 17(5) is the list of credits blocked even when that condition is met. The block would be meaningless if business use lifted it.

options.text: No, unless the car is registered in the firm's name
options.misconception: makes registration papers the deciding condition
options.why: Whose name is on the registration certificate never enters section 17(5). The block turns on what the vehicle is and what it is used for.

items.scenario: A consultancy buys a five-seater car for ₹22 lakh plus GST, used entirely by its partners for client visits. The accountant claims the input tax credit on the ground that the use is wholly for business.

items.stem: What is the GST position on these fees?

options.text: The company pays under reverse charge by debiting its input tax credit
options.misconception: discharges a reverse-charge liability through the credit ledger
options.why: Reverse charge must be paid through the cash ledger. The credit ledger can pay output tax on the company's own supplies, not the tax it owes as a recipient.

options.text: The company pays the GST under reverse charge, in cash
options.why: Legal services from an advocate to a business entity are notified under section 9(3), so the liability sits on the recipient. Reverse charge liability is discharged in cash — the company may then take credit of it, but cannot pay it out of credit.

options.text: The advocate should have charged GST on the bill
options.misconception: applies forward charge to a notified reverse-charge supply
options.why: For notified services the supplier neither charges nor collects. A bill without GST is the correct bill here; the tax travels on the company's own liability.

options.text: No GST arises, because legal services are exempt
options.misconception: stretches the small-recipient exemption to every recipient
options.why: The exemption covers advocates serving individuals and small business entities below the registration threshold. A ₹300 crore company is squarely outside it.

items.scenario: A manufacturing company with ₹300 crore turnover engages a senior advocate for a High Court matter and pays fees of ₹5 lakh. The advocate's bill shows no GST.

items.stem: Is registration required?

options.text: Yes, because every supplier of services must register from the first rupee
options.misconception: erases the threshold entirely for services
options.why: First-rupee registration applies to specific cases — inter-State taxable supply, e-commerce, reverse-charge recipients — not to services as a class.

options.text: No, not until turnover reaches ₹1.5 crore
options.misconception: mistakes the composition ceiling for the registration threshold
options.why: ₹1.5 crore is the composition scheme's eligibility ceiling — a choice available after registration, not a limit before it.

options.text: No, not until turnover reaches ₹40 lakh
options.misconception: applies the goods-only threshold to a service provider
options.why: The ₹40 lakh limit belongs to suppliers exclusively of goods in eligible States. One rupee of service supply keeps the ₹20 lakh limit in charge.

options.text: Yes — the services threshold of ₹20 lakh is crossed
options.why: A supplier of services takes the ₹20 lakh aggregate turnover limit, and ₹25 lakh is past it. Registration follows, with tax on supplies from the effective date.

items.scenario: A management consultant in Madhya Pradesh, supplying only services within the State, reaches aggregate turnover of ₹25 lakh during the year and asks whether registration is now compulsory.

items.stem: Can he make this supply while remaining in the scheme?

options.text: Yes, because his turnover is within the ₹1.5 crore ceiling
options.misconception: treats the turnover ceiling as the only eligibility condition
options.why: The ceiling is one condition of several. The inter-State bar is separate, and breaching it disqualifies regardless of how modest the turnover is.

options.text: No — inter-State outward supply ends composition eligibility
options.why: Section 10(2) bars a composition taxpayer from inter-State outward supplies. Shipping to Maharashtra means leaving the scheme and paying tax as a regular taxpayer, with the compliance that follows.

options.text: Yes, paying IGST on this order at the composition rate
options.misconception: extends the composition rate across State lines
options.why: There is no composition IGST. The scheme is a local-trade bargain, and the levy it charges exists only for intra-State supply.

options.text: Yes, if the Maharashtra buyer arranges his own transport from Indore
options.misconception: locates the supply by who carries the goods
options.why: Place of supply follows the movement's termination for delivery, not who pays the transporter. Goods bound for Maharashtra make an inter-State supply either way.

items.scenario: A composition dealer in Indore, selling hardware with turnover of ₹90 lakh, receives a large order from a buyer in Maharashtra and intends to supply it under the composition scheme.

items.stem: Which of these amounts is not added in arriving at the assessable value?

options.text: The selling commission of $2,000
options.misconception: excludes all commissions instead of only the buying commission
options.why: Selling commission is paid for the seller's benefit and is expressly added. The carve-out is for buying commission alone.

options.text: None of them — all payments connected with the import are added
options.misconception: adds everything rather than testing each payment against the rule
options.why: The rule works addition by addition, and buying commission is its stated exception. Adding everything overstates the value and the duty with it.

options.text: The buying commission of $1,500
options.why: Rule 10(1)(a) adds commissions and brokerage except buying commission. The importer's own agent works for the buyer, and paying him is part of the cost of buying, not part of the price of the goods.

options.text: The freight of $3,000
options.misconception: leaves transport out of a value that is built to the place of importation
options.why: Cost of transport to the place of importation is a Rule 10(2) addition. Assessable value is the landed value, and freight is part of landing the goods.

items.scenario: An importer's invoice shows goods at $50,000, selling commission of $2,000 paid to the exporter's agent, buying commission of $1,500 paid to the importer's own agent abroad, and freight of $3,000 to the Indian port.

items.stem: What level of assurance does an audit conducted in accordance with the Standards on Auditing obtain?

options.text: Reasonable assurance, which is a high but not absolute level of assurance
options.why: SA 200 defines the auditor's objective as obtaining reasonable assurance — a high level, but not absolute, because of the inherent limitations of an audit: the nature of financial reporting, the nature of audit procedures, and the need to complete the audit at a reasonable cost within a reasonable time.

options.text: Absolute assurance that the financial statements are free from material misstatement
options.misconception: promises absolute assurance, which no audit can give
options.why: Absolute assurance is unattainable. SA 200 states the inherent limitations expressly: audit evidence is persuasive rather than conclusive, and testing is selective rather than exhaustive.

options.text: A stated numerical probability that the financial statements are free from material misstatement
options.misconception: treats assurance as a probability the auditor is required to quantify
options.why: The Standards nowhere ask the auditor to express assurance as a percentage. Reasonable assurance is a qualitative concept about the sufficiency of evidence obtained, not a computed figure.

options.text: Moderate assurance, since "reasonable" means something less than high
options.misconception: reads "reasonable" as a lowering of the standard rather than a description of a high one
options.why: SA 200 uses "reasonable" to mean high. Moderate or limited assurance is the language of review engagements under SRE 2400, not of an audit.

items.stem: Can you accept the engagement?

options.text: Yes, if the promoter gives the acknowledgement orally instead
options.misconception: treats an oral acknowledgement as satisfying a written agreement of terms
options.why: SA 210 requires the agreed terms to be recorded in an engagement letter or other suitable written agreement. An oral assurance leaves nothing that can be pointed to later.

options.text: Yes, provided the audit report is modified to say management did not accept responsibility
options.misconception: converts a refusal to accept into a reporting matter
options.why: A modification describes the result of an audit that was performed. SA 210 stops the engagement earlier, at acceptance, precisely so the auditor is never in the position of reporting on an audit that lacked its foundation.

options.text: No, because management's agreement to its responsibilities is a precondition for an audit
options.why: The premise of an audit is that management acknowledges its responsibility for the financial statements, for internal control, and for providing access and information. Without that acknowledgement there is nothing for the audit to be an audit of, so SA 210 does not permit acceptance.

options.text: Yes, because the size of the company makes formal internal control unnecessary
options.misconception: confuses how elaborate the controls are with whether responsibility is accepted
options.why: The precondition is about who is responsible, not about how sophisticated the controls are. A small entity's controls may be simple; management still has to acknowledge them as its own.

items.scenario: A prospective client asks you to audit its financial statements but says it will not sign any acknowledgement of responsibility for internal control, on the ground that the company is small and the promoter handles everything personally.

items.stem: What should you do?

options.text: Accept, and use alternative procedures instead of confirmation and attendance
options.misconception: assumes alternative procedures can always replace a blocked procedure
options.why: Alternative procedures address a limitation the auditor meets during the audit, and they work only when they can actually produce the evidence. Here the restriction is imposed in advance and covers most of the balance sheet.

options.text: Accept, and report the restriction to those charged with governance
options.misconception: substitutes communication for the acceptance decision
options.why: Those charged with governance are, in this scenario, the source of the restriction. Reporting it back to them does not obtain the evidence or discharge the SA 210 test.

options.text: Decline the engagement, because the limitation would lead to a disclaimer of opinion
options.why: The two areas closed off are 70 per cent of total assets, so the auditor could not obtain sufficient appropriate evidence about anything material. SA 210 does not allow accepting an engagement whose known limitation will end in a disclaimer, unless law requires it.

options.text: Accept, perform what you can, and issue a disclaimer of opinion
options.misconception: accepts a doomed engagement on the basis that the report will say so
options.why: Knowingly accepting an audit that cannot produce an opinion lends the auditor's name to an exercise with no outcome. That is the outcome SA 210 exists to prevent, which is why the test is applied at acceptance.

items.scenario: Before appointing you, a company tells you that you may not circularise trade receivables or attend the inventory count, because both would disturb its customers and its plant. Receivables and inventory together are 70 per cent of total assets.

items.stem: Where does responsibility for the quality of this engagement sit?

options.text: With the firm, through its system of quality management
options.misconception: substitutes the firm-level system for the engagement-level responsibility
options.why: The firm's system is a separate requirement under SQM 1 and sits alongside this one. It supports the engagement partner rather than replacing them.

options.text: With the manager, who performed the detailed review
options.misconception: moves responsibility to whoever did the work
options.why: The manager is accountable within the firm for the review performed, but the standard does not shift the engagement partner's overall responsibility onto the person delegated to.

options.text: With the engagement partner, who retains overall responsibility however the work is delegated
options.why: SA 220 (Revised) places overall responsibility for managing and achieving quality on the engagement partner. Delegating review work is normal and expected; delegating the responsibility for quality is not possible.

options.text: Shared equally between the engagement partner and the engagement quality reviewer
options.misconception: treats an independent review as a transfer of responsibility
options.why: An engagement quality review is an objective evaluation of significant judgements. It does not reduce or share the engagement partner's overall responsibility for quality.

items.scenario: An audit is staffed with a manager, two seniors and three articles. The engagement partner visits the client twice, reviews the summary memorandum and signs the report. The detailed review of every working paper was done by the manager.

items.stem: Within what period must the final audit file ordinarily be assembled after the auditor's report is dated?

options.text: 90 days
options.misconception: confuses assembly with the longer periods that govern retention
options.why: Retention runs for years, not 90 days; assembly is the 60-day requirement. The two are separate obligations under SA 230.

options.text: 30 days
options.misconception: carries over a shorter statutory filing period as if it governed file assembly
options.why: No provision of SA 230 sets 30 days. The number is imported from unrelated filing deadlines.

options.text: 60 days
options.why: SA 230 sets an outer limit of ordinarily not more than 60 days after the date of the auditor's report for completing the administrative assembly of the final file.

options.text: Before the auditor's report is signed
options.misconception: treats assembly as a precondition to signing rather than an administrative step after it
options.why: SA 230 measures the period from the date of the auditor's report, which presupposes the report is already dated. Assembly is administrative and adds no new evidence.

items.stem: What does SA 230 require when you add to the file after the report date?

options.text: The audit report must be reissued to reflect the additional documentation
options.misconception: confuses completing the file with changing the opinion
options.why: Writing up a discussion that informed an opinion already reached changes nothing about the opinion. Reissuing a report is for facts discovered after the date that would have changed it.

options.text: Nothing may be added after the report date, so the paper must be left out
options.misconception: reads the assembly period as a freeze on the file
options.why: The file is assembled after the report is signed; that is what the assembly period is for. The rule governs how additions are recorded, not whether they may be made.

options.text: Nothing, provided the addition is made within sixty days of the report date
options.misconception: treats the assembly period as a window in which changes need no record
options.why: The period bounds when assembly must finish. It does not suspend the documentation requirement for changes made inside it.

options.text: Document when and by whom the addition was made and reviewed, and why it was made
options.why: Additions during the assembly period are allowed — assembling the file is administrative. What SA 230 requires is that the change be visible: the reasons for it, and who made and reviewed it and when, so the file cannot be quietly rewritten after the event.

items.scenario: Two weeks after signing the audit report, you realise a working paper recording your discussion with the finance director about a provision was never filed. You write it up now and add it to the file.

items.stem: How should you treat the risk of management override of controls?

options.text: As a significant risk only where the assessment shows the control environment to be weak
options.misconception: makes a mandatory risk conditional on the strength of controls
options.why: SA 240 attaches no such condition. The risk arises from management's position of authority, not from any deficiency in the controls it is able to override.

options.text: As a significant risk only in the audits of listed entities
options.misconception: confines a requirement that applies to all audits to listed entities alone
options.why: SA 240 draws no distinction by class of entity here. If anything the risk is higher in owner-managed entities, where fewer people stand between management and the accounting records.

options.text: As a presumption that may be rebutted with documented reasons, as with revenue recognition
options.misconception: borrows the rebuttable revenue presumption and applies it where the Standard allows no rebuttal
options.why: SA 240 makes only the revenue-recognition fraud risk rebuttable. The management-override requirement is stated unconditionally and there is no mechanism in the Standard for setting it aside.

options.text: As a significant risk present in every audit, so the required responses are performed regardless of the control environment
options.why: SA 240 requires the auditor to treat management override as a significant risk in all audits. Management is uniquely placed to override controls that otherwise operate effectively, so a strong control environment does not remove the risk — it is precisely what management is able to override.

items.scenario: A client has a well-designed control environment, no history of fraud, and an audit committee that meets regularly. Your engagement team argues that testing journal entries for management override adds nothing this year.

items.stem: What is the status of the presumed risk of fraud in revenue recognition?

options.text: It is presumed, but the auditor may rebut it and must document the reasons for that conclusion
options.why: SA 240 requires the auditor to presume fraud risks in revenue recognition, while permitting rebuttal where the presumption is not applicable in the circumstances. Where it is rebutted, the Standard requires the reasons to be documented.

options.text: It applies uniformly to every revenue stream, so no analysis of which streams carry the risk is needed
options.misconception: applies the presumption as a blanket rule instead of identifying which revenue assertions carry the risk
options.why: SA 240 requires the auditor to identify which types of revenue, revenue transactions or assertions give rise to the risk. A blanket assumption skips the identification the Standard asks for.

options.text: It may be rebutted only with the approval of those charged with governance
options.misconception: makes a professional judgement subject to a governance approval the Standard never requires
options.why: The rebuttal is the auditor's judgement, documented in the working papers. SA 240 requires documentation, not consent.

options.text: It cannot be rebutted in any circumstances
options.misconception: makes the revenue presumption as absolute as the management-override requirement
options.why: SA 240 phrases the two differently on purpose. Revenue is rebuttable in the circumstances of the engagement; management override is not.

items.stem: Why does SA 240 require you to test journal entries in every audit, and what makes these ones urgent?

options.text: Because journal entries are always the largest source of error in any accounting system
options.misconception: justifies the procedure by frequency of error rather than by the override risk
options.why: The requirement is not about where errors happen most. It exists because override is the one risk that cannot be controlled away, since it is the controls themselves that are being overridden.

options.text: Because the auditor is required to detect all fraud, and journals are where fraud is hidden
options.misconception: overstates the auditor's responsibility from reasonable assurance to detection of all fraud
options.why: The auditor obtains reasonable assurance that the statements are free from material misstatement, whether from fraud or error. That is not a duty to detect all fraud, and SA 240 does not create one.

options.text: It is not required in every audit; it is required only where fraud risk factors have been identified
options.misconception: makes a mandatory response conditional on identifying risk factors first
options.why: SA 240 requires the journal entry testing regardless. Management override is presumed to be a risk in every entity, so the response is not conditional on anything being spotted first.

options.text: Because management can override controls that otherwise operate effectively, and these entries carry the hallmarks of override
options.why: SA 240 treats management override as a risk present in every entity, however good the controls, because the people who can override them are the people who run them. Testing journal entries is one of the required responses. These entries carry the classic markers — posted at the period end, outside the normal process, approved by one person, and explained by a narration that explains nothing.

items.scenario: A company posts 41 manual journal entries on 31 March 2026, all after the normal cut-off, all approved by the chief financial officer alone, and all with the narration "regrouping". Their net effect increases profit by ₹3.7 crore.

items.stem: What is your responsibility under SA 250 for compliance with the environmental clearance?

options.text: No responsibility at all, because compliance with environmental law is management's concern
options.misconception: reads the split as duty versus no duty, rather than two different duties
options.why: Both categories carry a duty. The second is narrower, not absent: SA 250 still requires enquiry of management and inspection of correspondence with the licensing authority.

options.text: Report the matter to the regulator before completing the audit
options.misconception: jumps to external reporting before the standard's own procedures
options.why: Reporting outside the entity is a separate question that arises only after non-compliance is identified or suspected, and is governed by law and by SA 250's later paragraphs. It is not the auditor's responsibility for compliance as such.

options.text: Perform specified procedures to help identify non-compliance, without obtaining evidence about compliance itself
options.why: The clearance is fundamental to the operating aspects of the business but has no direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures, so it falls in SA 250's second category. There the auditor's responsibility is limited to specified procedures — enquiring of management and inspecting correspondence with the relevant licensing authority — rather than obtaining evidence about compliance.

options.text: Obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about compliance with every condition
options.misconception: applies the higher first-category duty to a law with no direct effect on the figures
options.why: That is the duty for the first category only — laws that directly determine material amounts and disclosures. Extending it to every law fundamental to operations would make the auditor a compliance inspector, which SA 250 expressly does not do.

items.scenario: You are auditing a chemical manufacturer. The company holds an environmental clearance whose conditions govern how effluent is discharged. Breaching those conditions can lead to the plant being shut down, but the clearance does not itself determine any figure recognised in the financial statements.

items.stem: Which of these must be communicated to those charged with governance?

options.text: Nothing further, provided the matters have been discussed with management
options.misconception: treats management as a substitute for those charged with governance
options.why: The two are different bodies with different roles, and they overlap only in some entities. SA 260 (Revised) addresses the communication to those charged with governance specifically.

options.text: Only the findings from the audit, since scope is the auditor's own affair
options.misconception: restricts the communication to findings when the Standard also requires planning matters
options.why: SA 260 (Revised) lists the auditor's responsibilities, the planned scope and timing, and significant findings as separate required communications. Reporting only findings omits two of the three.

options.text: Nothing, unless the entity is listed
options.misconception: treats a requirement that applies to all audits as one confined to listed entities
options.why: Only the independence communication in SA 260 (Revised) is confined to listed entities. Scope and timing are communicated in every audit.

options.text: The planned scope and timing of the audit
options.why: SA 260 (Revised) requires the auditor to communicate an overview of the planned scope and timing of the audit. Communication runs in both directions and before the work as well as after it, so that governance understands what the audit will and will not cover.

items.stem: What does SA 265 require you to do?

options.text: Communicate the three significant deficiencies to management alone
options.misconception: stops at management where the Standard requires the communication to reach governance
options.why: SA 265 directs significant deficiencies to those charged with governance. Communicating only to management withholds them from the body responsible for overseeing management.

options.text: Communicate all eleven deficiencies in writing to those charged with governance
options.misconception: raises every deficiency to the level the Standard reserves for significant ones
options.why: Only significant deficiencies go in writing to those charged with governance. Other deficiencies of sufficient importance go to management, at the appropriate level.

options.text: Communicate the three significant deficiencies orally at the closing meeting
options.misconception: substitutes an oral communication where the Standard requires writing
options.why: SA 265 specifies written communication for significant deficiencies. An oral briefing may supplement it but cannot replace it.

options.text: Communicate the three significant deficiencies in writing to those charged with governance on a timely basis
options.why: SA 265 requires significant deficiencies to be communicated in writing and on a timely basis to those charged with governance. The written form exists so that the matter is recorded and can be acted on; timeliness exists so it can be acted on while it still matters.

items.scenario: During the audit you identify eleven deficiencies in internal control. Three are significant deficiencies in your professional judgement; the remaining eight are minor.

items.stem: Who bears responsibility for that misstatement?

options.text: Firm A alone, and no element of the audit carries joint responsibility
options.misconception: removes the joint element entirely and leaves undivided work unowned
options.why: The undivided work — here the treasury operations, and the report itself — is jointly and severally the responsibility of both. Individual responsibility exists alongside joint responsibility, not instead of it.

options.text: Both firms jointly, because joint auditors are responsible for the whole audit without division
options.misconception: collapses divided work into joint responsibility and leaves division of work with no meaning
options.why: SA 299 (Revised) provides expressly for division of work and attaches individual responsibility to it. If everything were joint, the Standard's division provisions would do nothing.

options.text: The firm that signs first, as the principal joint auditor
options.misconception: invents a principal joint auditor, a rank SA 299 does not create
options.why: SA 299 (Revised) recognises no hierarchy among joint auditors. Order of signature carries no consequence for responsibility.

options.text: Firm A alone, because the northern division was the work divided to it; both firms remain jointly and severally responsible for the undivided treasury work
options.why: SA 299 (Revised) makes each joint auditor responsible for the work allocated to that auditor, and all joint auditors jointly and severally responsible for work not divided and for decisions taken together, including the audit report.

items.scenario: Two firms are joint auditors of a company. The work is divided by division: Firm A takes the northern division, Firm B the southern. Neither firm's division covers the group's treasury operations, which both firms address together. A misstatement is later found in the northern division's revenue.

items.stem: What follows from determining that an identified risk is a significant risk?

options.text: They may be addressed by substantive procedures alone, with no need to understand the related controls
options.misconception: skips the mandatory understanding of controls by going straight to substantive work
options.why: SA 315 (Revised) requires the understanding of related controls whatever the planned response. The response is a separate question, governed by SA 330.

options.text: Significant risks arise only from fraud
options.misconception: confines significant risks to fraud when error can equally produce one
options.why: Fraud risks are always significant risks, but the category is wider. Complex estimates and unusual transactions give rise to significant risks of error.

options.text: Every high-value balance is a significant risk, so materiality alone identifies them
options.misconception: reduces a judgement about the nature of a risk to the size of the balance
options.why: SA 315 (Revised) points to complexity, subjectivity, significant judgement, unusual transactions and related-party dealings — none of which is measured in rupees. A large but routine balance may carry no significant risk at all.

options.text: It requires special audit consideration, and the auditor must obtain an understanding of the entity's controls relevant to that risk
options.why: SA 315 (Revised) defines a significant risk as one requiring special audit consideration, and requires the auditor to evaluate the design and determine the implementation of the controls relevant to it. Understanding those controls is what makes a targeted response possible.

items.stem: Why does this transaction give rise to a significant risk?

options.text: It is an unusual related party transaction outside the normal course of business, with a significant effect on the reported result
options.why: SA 315 (Revised) points to unusual transactions and related-party dealings as indicators. Every indicator is present at once here: the counterparty is related, the transaction is outside normal operations, its timing is close to the year end, and it changes the headline result.

options.text: It does not; a completed sale supported by a registered deed is fully verifiable
options.misconception: mistakes ease of vouching for absence of risk
options.why: The deed proves a sale occurred. It says nothing about whether the price was arm's length, whether the substance matches the form, or whether the timing was chosen to produce the result — which is where the risk lives.

options.text: Because the company is listed, and all listed company transactions carry significant risk
options.misconception: attaches the risk to the entity's status rather than to the transaction
options.why: Listing brings its own reporting and independence requirements, but it does not make every transaction a significant risk. The assessment is made transaction by transaction.

options.text: Because the gain is large in rupee terms
options.misconception: reduces a judgement about the nature of a risk to the size of the amount
options.why: Size alone does not make a significant risk. A large but routine sale carries none. What matters here is that the transaction is related-party, non-routine and result-changing.
